title: The Cockatoos Across the Strait

lines.text: A naturalist sailed fifteen miles and lost the woodpeckers.
Three months of collecting. Not one. The answer wasn't on either island.
Alfred Russel Wallace had come from Bali to the next island, Lombok.
On Bali he had seen barbets, fruit-thrushes and woodpeckers.
On Lombok: cockatoos, honeysuckers, brush-turkeys. Australian kinds of bird.
Same soils. Similar climate. So it isn't the land.
Wallace looked under the water instead.
To the west, the sea is shallow. Rarely more than forty fathoms, by his account.
Shallow enough, he reasoned, that those islands were joined to Asia not long ago.
To the east, the water is far deeper, which pointed to a long separation.
In 1868, Thomas Henry Huxley named the boundary Wallace's Line.
Nature's sharpest borders can follow old gaps in the sea that animals could not cross.
Today's number: fifteen. The miles between two histories of life.

caption: Bali and Lombok look alike, yet one has Asian birds and the other Australian ones. The border is Wallace's Line, and it follows deep water. A true story, fact-checked. Tomorrow: Literature. Curiouser No. 10
